opus-5.5.text:
My read is that Physical Intelligence has been fairly skeptical of simulation as the main engine for training general-purpose robot policies, and I think that skepticism is quite deliberate.

Their bet has mostly been on real-world data: teleoperation across many different robots, many tasks, many environments, then training one large vision-language-action model on all of it. The idea is that the messiness of the real world, like deformable objects, contact, lighting, and all the small physical details, is exactly what simulators struggle to model. If you train heavily in sim, you spend a lot of effort closing the sim-to-real gap. They seem to have decided it's more direct to collect real data and let scale and diversity do the work.

I wouldn't call it a rejection of simulation, though. It's more of a prioritization. Simulation is still very useful for evaluation, for testing ideas cheaply, for some reinforcement learning, and for tasks like locomotion, where the physics is relatively well understood. Where it's weakest is dexterous manipulation in unstructured homes: folding laundry, wiping a table, packing a box. That's the kind of task they care most about.

So I'd frame their position as: simulation is a tool, not the foundation. The foundation is real-world data plus pretrained knowledge from internet-scale models. Whether that holds as world models and generative simulation improve is an open question. If learned simulators get good enough to produce physically plausible interaction data, I think many teams, possibly including them, would bring simulation back into the training loop in a much bigger way. For now, though, their philosophy is basically "the real world is the best simulator."

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Physical Intelligence as skeptical of simulation as a training foundation and says it may use simulation more if learned simulators improve. It does not state that the company now strongly recognizes internally that it needs simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
My read is that Physical Intelligence is fairly skeptical of simulation, at least as the main engine for building general robot policies. Their bet is on real-world data. The whole thesis behind π0 and what came after is that the way you get a foundation model for robots is the same way you got one for language: collect a huge, diverse pile of real data and train a big model on it. Simulation sits uneasily with that.

The core problem is the sim-to-real gap, and it's not just visuals. Rendering has gotten very good, so the pixel-level gap is shrinking. The harder gap is physics, especially contact. Think about the tasks they care about: folding laundry, loading a dishwasher, wiping a table, handling deformable objects. Cloth, liquids, friction between a gripper and a slightly damp plate. Simulators are bad at exactly these things, and those are the things that make manipulation hard. If you train in a world where cloth behaves wrong, you learn a policy that is confidently wrong in the real world.

So their attitude, as I understand it, is roughly: simulation is a tool, not a data source. It's useful for evaluation, for sanity-checking a policy before putting it on hardware, maybe for navigation or locomotion where the physics is more forgiving. But for dexterous manipulation they'd rather pay the cost of teleoperation and real-world collection, because every hour of real data is an hour of true physics.

There's also a practical argument. Real-world data collection scales with people and robots, which is expensive but predictable. Simulation scales with engineering effort to make each new task and asset realistic, and that effort doesn't amortize well across the long tail of household objects. A lot of the field learned this the hard way with earlier sim-heavy approaches.

I'd add one nuance. I don't think they'd say simulation is useless forever. If world models or learned simulators get good enough to generate realistic contact-rich interaction, that's effectively synthetic data, and they'd happily use it. But that's a different thing from a hand-built physics engine. Right now the honest answer is that the real world is the best simulator we have, and PI is organized around that assumption.

r001.rationale: The response describes Physical Intelligence as skeptical of simulation and says it currently prioritizes real-world data. Its conditional openness to future learned simulators does not state that PI now strongly recognizes an internal need for simulation.

astra-6.text:
My impression is that Physical Intelligence takes a pragmatic view of simulation: it can be useful, but the real test is whether it improves a robot’s performance in the physical world. I wouldn’t interpret that as being against simulation.

For manipulation, the hard part is often the interaction itself—contact, friction, deformable objects. A simulated environment can look convincing while getting those details wrong. So the question is how much useful learning transfers, and how much real-world data you still need to close the gap.

I’d distinguish between saying simulation isn’t sufficient and saying it isn’t valuable. Those are very different positions. Without a specific statement from them to discuss, I’d be cautious about attributing a stronger position than that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says simulation can be useful, but does not state that Physical Intelligence now strongly recognizes internally that it needs simulation; it explicitly cautions against attributing a stronger position without a specific statement.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that they’re pragmatic about simulation. It’s useful for testing ideas and generating experience at scale, but the key question is how much that experience improves performance in the real world.

For manipulation, that’s a difficult question. Contact, friction, deformable objects—these are all things where a small mismatch can change the outcome. So I wouldn’t interpret an emphasis on real-world data as a rejection of simulation. It’s more about where they think the most useful training signal comes from today.

The two can be complementary: use simulation where it transfers well, and use real-world experience to capture what the simulator misses. That’s my interpretation, rather than a claim about their internal roadmap.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulation as useful and complementary to real-world experience, but does not state that Physical Intelligence now strongly recognizes internally that it needs simulation.
